docs.title: rn-forge-auth
docs.text:
rn-forge-auth holds authentication and authorization primitives, built on rn-forge-web: the identity, account-resolution and authorization-context contracts, Principal and Requirement, the Authenticator and Authorizer contracts, session, transaction and replay stores, the login flow and its OIDC, OAuth 2.0, password and development providers, and the OIDC token profiles.

The base install gives the core, rn_forge.auth. The oidc extra adds pyjwt[crypto] and authlib for the adapter, rn_forge.auth.oidc, and for the fake provider in rn_forge.auth.testing; the redis extra adds redis for rn_forge.auth.redis. The core imports none of them.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
• Authentication and authorization shows how the pieces fit and covers installing the core and its extras.
  • Contracts, Login providers, Token profiles, Stores and Testing cover each subsystem.
  • The API reference is generated from the docstrings.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: Notable changes to rn-forge-auth, newest first, in the Keep a Changelog format.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• rn_forge.auth.conformance: CASES, one SecurityControlCase per row of the design's security controls, case_by_id, and tagged_tests, which finds the tests of a suite that carry @pytest.mark.security_control("<id>"). Both framework bindings' suites fail when a case has no tagged test.
  • rn_forge.auth.audit (audit, AUDIT_LOGGER), the audit event helper on the rn_forge.audit.auth AppLogger channel, which both framework bindings emit their auth events through.
  • LoginFlow.complete returns CompletedLogin (identity and the consumed transaction's return_to). ExternalIdentity gains id_token, set by OidcProvider only with rp_initiated_logout, so a binding can keep it in the session.
  • The rn-forge-auth package: the rn_forge.auth core, the oidc extra for the rn_forge.auth.oidc adapter and the redis extra for the rn_forge.auth.redis adapter.
  • Principal, Requirement, Authenticator, AsyncAuthenticator, Authorizer, ScopeAuthorizer and principal_from_claims, moved from rn-forge-web into the rn_forge.auth core, and OidcAuthenticator, moved from rn_forge.web.oidc into rn_forge.auth.oidc.
  • JwtVerifier, discover_oidc, fetch_json, FetchJson, OidcConfiguration and TokenVerificationError, moved from rn_forge.commons.integration.auth into rn_forge.auth.oidc. JwtVerifier gains from_jwks_url.
  • The identity and authorization contracts: ExternalIdentity, IdentityProvider, ProviderKind, LoginStart, LoginTransaction, SessionInfo, AccountResolver, AccountRejected, AuthorizationContext, AuthorizationContextProvider and ResourcePolicy.
  • requirement_for, effective_permissions and Mechanism, and DEFAULT_PERMISSION_ACTION_MAP, moved from rn-forge-django.
  • AuthorizationContextCache, which caches an AuthorizationContextProvider by account and authorization version with a TTL, with AuthorizationVersions, InMemoryAuthorizationVersions and AccountStateWriter.
  • IdTokenVerifier, the ID-token profile, which runs Authlib's CodeIDToken and checks auth_time against max_age, and LogoutTokenVerifier, the back-channel logout-token profile, which checks typ, the iat window and a single-use jti.
  • JwtVerifier and OidcAuthenticator take mode ("rfc9068" or "rfc7519") and login_client_id; the latter is refused as an audience outside RFC 9068 mode.
  • ReplayStore and InMemoryReplayStore, the single-use and revoked-sid records.
  • TransactionStore and SessionStore, with InMemoryTransactionStore and InMemorySessionStore, which are not safe across processes.
  • RedisTransactionStore, RedisSessionStore, RedisReplayStore and RedisAuthorizationVersions in rn_forge.auth.redis.
  • validate_return_to and InvalidReturnTo, which accept only a relative path under configured prefixes; SessionBody, the camelCase /auth/session body; and CallbackError, the closed list of callback error codes.
  • rn_forge.auth.testing, behind the oidc extra: FakeOidcProvider, an in-process OIDC provider with discovery, key rotation, authorization, token and UserInfo endpoints and logout tokens, and Faults, a switch for each OIDC failure.
  • The login adapters:
  • LoginFlow and LoginFailed, the framework-neutral login flow, and LoginRequest, the thin request protocol providers read. begin validates return_to and saves the transaction for 600 seconds; complete consumes it once, rejects a missing, expired, used or foreign transaction, and ends every failure in a LoginFailed carrying a CallbackError.
  • OidcProvider in rn_forge.auth.oidc, the OIDC login provider over Authlib's OAuth2Session: discovery with the issuer check, state, nonce, PKCE S256, the RFC 9207 iss check, max_age, ID-token verification and UserInfo with a sub check. default_claim_mapper, a claim_mapper hook and a token_hook (the only receiver of the upstream tokens, UpstreamTokens) shape the result. No token, code or verifier is logged.
  • OidcProvider.oauth2 and OAuth2Endpoints, the same provider for an OAuth 2.0 server that issues no ID token: it keeps state and PKCE, sends no nonce, calls the user endpoint with the access token and maps the result (subject_field picks the subject, numbers are stringified). The iss response check applies only with response_issuer.
  • OidcProvider.logout_redirect, which returns the discovered end_session_endpoint with id_token_hint, post_logout_redirect_uri and client_id when the provider is built with rp_initiated_logout=True, and BackchannelLogout with LogoutRevocation, which validate a back-channel logout token and return the (issuer, sid) to revoke, or the account whose session version to bump for a token with only sub.
  • PasswordIdentityProvider and DevelopmentIdentityProvider in rn_forge.auth.local, with PasswordVerifier, DevelopmentAccount and DevelopmentModeRequired. Neither needs an extra.
  • OidcConfiguration.metadata, the whole discovery document.
  • FakeOidcProvider gains oauth2_only and auth_age, and Faults gains userinfo_error.
  • Optional Keycloak tests of the broker profile under tests/broker/, run by the non-gating broker-profile workflow.
  • Guides for the contracts, the login providers (including connecting a SAML IdP through a broker), the token profiles, the stores, and the fake provider with the broker tests.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• Breaking: Principal gains external_subject, permissions, attributes, auth_time and amr, and mechanism is the Mechanism literal ("session", "bearer" or "basic") instead of str.
  • Breaking: Requirement gains any_permission and all_permissions, checked against Principal.permissions, and loses any_role and all_roles.
  • Breaking: JwtVerifier rejects a token carrying nonce or events, and enforces typ: JWT or none by default, at+jwt in RFC 9068 mode.
  • JwtVerifier takes its keys from PyJWT's PyJWKClient, replacing JwksCache. from_issuer and from_jwks_url take lifespan (default 300 seconds) and cooldown_duration (default 30 seconds) in place of max_age, and from_jwks_url no longer takes fetch: only the discovery document uses fetch_json.
  • The oidc extra is pyjwt[crypto] with authlib>=1.9.1 and joserfc>=1.7.7; it requires PyJWT 2.15.0 or later.
  • The package declares the MIT licence and is published to PyPI.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
• Authentication and authorization — how the pieces fit, from identity provider to ResourcePolicy; installing the core and the extras; and how the package meets rn-forge-web and the framework packages.
  • Contracts — identity providers, account resolution, the authorization context and its cache, Principal and Requirement, permissions and the scope limit, resource policy, return_to and the session body.
  • Login providers — LoginFlow; the OIDC, OAuth 2.0, password and development providers; back-channel logout; and connecting a SAML IdP through a broker.
  • Token profiles — the access-token, ID-token and logout-token verifiers, their modes, the login-client rule and key-set caching.
  • Stores — the transaction, session, replay and version stores, in memory and on Redis.
  • Testing — the in-process fake OIDC provider and its failure switches.

docs.title: Contracts
docs.text: The core, rn_forge.auth, is a set of contracts and the values they exchange. This guide walks them in the order a request meets them; the overview shows how they connect. For tokens, see Token profiles; for server-side state, see Stores.

docs.title: Identity providers and external identities
docs.text:
An IdentityProvider[RequestT] is one login method, generic over the framework's native request type. It has an id and a kind (ProviderKind: "oidc", "oauth2", "password" or "development") and three methods:

  • begin(request, *, return_to) returns a LoginStart: the LoginTransaction to persist and the redirect_url to send the browser to, or None when the provider takes a form instead, as password login does.
  • complete(request, transaction) validates the provider's response against the transaction and returns an ExternalIdentity.
  • logout_redirect(session, *, post_logout_redirect) returns the provider's logout URL, or None for a local logout only.

ExternalIdentity is a verified identity asserted by a provider: provider, issuer, subject, and optionally email, email_verified, name, picture, groups, attributes, auth_time, amr and session_ref (the OIDC sid). Everything after this value is framework-neutral. LoginTransaction is the state of one login in flight (state, nonce, code_verifier, return_to), saved in a TransactionStore between begin and complete.

SessionInfo is what a login session stores: the internal account_id, the session_version at login, how the user authenticated, and expires_at. It holds no permissions; they are looked up per request (see Authorization context).

docs.title: Account resolution
docs.text:
An AccountResolver maps an ExternalIdentity to an internal account ID. resolve(identity) links, provisions or rejects a login and returns the account ID; it raises AccountRejected when the login may not proceed. lookup(issuer, subject) returns the linked account ID, or None, and never provisions.

AccountRejected carries a reason for logs. The user is never shown it: the callback sends one of the CallbackError codes instead (see Return targets, the session body and callback errors).

docs.title: Authorization context and cache
docs.text:
An AuthorizationContext is an account's current authorization data: active (whether it may authenticate), session_version, permissions, roles (a display hint and an input to your provider) and attributes (inputs to attribute-based rules such as tenant or location). An AuthorizationContextProvider returns it from an account ID with resolve(account_id).

A session holds only the account ID and its session_version. On each request the binding fetches the current context, checks active and that the session's version still matches, and builds the Principal from the context. Revoking a permission, deactivating an account or bumping the session version therefore takes effect on the next request, with no session to edit.

docs.title: Caching contexts
docs.text:
AuthorizationContextCache wraps an AuthorizationContextProvider so a request does not recompute the account's permissions every time. It keeps one entry per account in process memory and serves it while the account's authorization version and the global version are unchanged and the entry is younger than the TTL (60 seconds by default).

cache = AuthorizationContextCache(provider, ttl=timedelta(seconds=30), writer=writer)

cache.invalidate("acct-1")   # one account's permissions changed
cache.invalidate_all()       # a role definition or an import changed many
cache.set_active("acct-1", False)          # writer, then invalidate
new_version = cache.bump_session_version("acct-1")

Use set_active and bump_session_version for the two values that revoke access, so no cached context outlives the change; they need an AccountStateWriter that the application implements. A change made behind the cache's back, such as a direct database edit, applies once the TTL passes.

The default InMemoryAuthorizationVersions is not shared across processes, so with several workers a bump reaches only the worker that made it and the others rely on the TTL. A shared AuthorizationVersions implementation fixes that.

docs.title: Principal and Requirement
docs.text:
Principal is the verified caller, a frozen dataclass. subject is the only required field. permissions holds the effective permissions, scopes the token's delegated scopes (empty for a session), and roles, tenant and attributes the application's authorization data. mechanism is "session", "bearer" or "basic" and defaults to "bearer"; claims keeps every verified claim; external_subject, auth_time and amr record how the caller authenticated.

Requirement is a declarative access check with four frozen sets. The sets are ANDed together; the members of an any_* set are ORed:

Field Satisfied when any_scope empty, or the principal holds at least one of them all_scopes the principal holds every one of them any_permission empty, or the principal's permissions include at least one of them all_permissions the principal's permissions include every one of them

An empty Requirement() is satisfied by any principal: it means "authenticated", not "denied". Routes require permissions, never roles; the scope clauses can only narrow access further.

from rn_forge.auth import Principal, Requirement

requirement = Requirement(any_scope=frozenset({"orders:read", "orders:admin"}))
caller = Principal(subject="u-1", scopes=frozenset({"orders:read"}))
requirement.is_satisfied_by(caller)  # True

docs.title: Permissions and the scope limit
docs.text:
requirement_for builds the requirement for a resource key and an action: requirement_for("orders", "partial_update") requires orders.update. DEFAULT_PERMISSION_ACTION_MAP maps the action names; an action_map argument overrides entries of it, and an action named by neither map is used as is.

A token's scopes limit, and never grant, permissions. effective_permissions returns a session or basic caller's account permissions unchanged, and for a bearer caller keeps only the permissions that its scopes allow through your scope map. A scope the map does not name allows nothing.

from rn_forge.auth import effective_permissions, requirement_for

permissions = effective_permissions(
    frozenset({"orders.read", "orders.update"}),
    mechanism="bearer",
    scopes=frozenset({"orders:read"}),
    scope_map={"orders:read": frozenset({"orders.list", "orders.read"})},
)  # frozenset({"orders.read"})
requirement_for("orders", "partial_update")  # needs orders.update: denied

docs.title: Authenticators and authorizers
docs.text:
The contracts are runtime-checkable protocols.

  • Authenticator.authenticate(*, credentials) turns a Credentials into a Principal. AsyncAuthenticator is the awaitable counterpart. A failure raises rn_forge.web.AuthenticationFailed; its message must not say which part of the credentials was wrong.
  • Authorizer.authorize(principal, *, requires) returns when the request may proceed and raises rn_forge.web.PermissionDenied when it may not. It never raises AuthenticationFailed: the caller is already authenticated, which is the line between 401 and 403.

ScopeAuthorizer is the shipped Authorizer. It evaluates the Requirement and raises PermissionDenied with a fixed message. Pass log to be told about each refusal; it is called as log("authorization.denied", context), where context holds subject, mechanism and required.

from rn_forge.auth import ScopeAuthorizer

authorizer = ScopeAuthorizer(log=lambda message, context: print(message, context))
authorizer.authorize(caller, requires=requirement)

docs.title: Mapping claims to a principal
docs.text:
principal_from_claims(claims, *, mechanism="bearer") is the default mapping from already-verified claims:

Principal Claim subject sub, required issuer iss scopes scope (space-delimited string) and scp (string or list), combined roles roles (a list) tenant tid

It raises AuthenticationFailed when sub is missing or empty. A claim of the wrong type for issuer or tenant is ignored, not an error.

An identity provider that keeps roles elsewhere, such as Keycloak's realm_access.roles, needs its own mapping. Any callable from verified claims to a Principal works; Principal.claims still holds the whole token:

from dataclasses import replace

from rn_forge.auth import Principal, principal_from_claims


def keycloak_principal(claims: dict[str, object]) -> Principal:
    principal = principal_from_claims(claims)
    realm = claims.get("realm_access")
    roles = realm.get("roles", ()) if isinstance(realm, dict) else ()
    return replace(principal, roles=frozenset(str(role) for role in roles))

Hand it to OidcAuthenticator as claims_to_principal.

docs.title: Resource policy
docs.text:
A Requirement decides whether a caller may reach a route. A ResourcePolicy decides what the caller may do with a particular object or set of objects:

  • allows(principal, action, resource) returns whether the principal may perform the action on one resource.
  • scope(principal, action, query) returns the query narrowed to what the principal may perform the action on, such as a queryset filtered by tenant.

It is generic over the resource and query types, so the application chooses both. The core supplies the protocol only.

docs.title: Return targets, the session body and callback errors
docs.text:
validate_return_to accepts a return_to only when it is a relative path under one of the configured prefixes, matched on whole segments:

from rn_forge.auth import InvalidReturnTo, validate_return_to

try:
    target = validate_return_to(raw, prefixes=["/app"])
except InvalidReturnTo:
    target = "/app"

It rejects absolute and scheme-relative URLs, backslashes, control characters, percent-encoded slashes, backslashes and dots in the path, .. segments and paths outside the prefixes. A query string and fragment may follow the path. The caller falls back to a default on InvalidReturnTo.

SessionBody.build(session, context, name=..., email=..., picture=...) makes the /auth/session body; subject is the internal account ID. to_json() returns camelCase keys, RFC 3339 UTC timestamps, sorted roles, permissions and amr, and leaves out absent optional fields. The keys of attributes are converted from snake_case to camelCase at every depth.

CallbackError is the closed list of codes a failed callback sends to the error route: access_denied, account_not_provisioned and login_failed.

docs.title: Login providers
docs.text:
A login provider turns a framework request into an ExternalIdentity. LoginFlow runs the providers for a framework binding. Every provider implements IdentityProvider, so a binding handles OIDC, OAuth 2.0, password and development logins the same way.

Provider Module Extra OidcProvider rn_forge.auth.oidc oidc OidcProvider.oauth2(...) rn_forge.auth.oidc oidc PasswordIdentityProvider rn_forge.auth.local none DevelopmentIdentityProvider rn_forge.auth.local none

rn_forge.auth.oidc needs the oidc extra and is imported directly. The rn_forge.auth facade re-exports LoginFlow, LoginFailed, LoginRequest and the rn_forge.auth.local providers.

docs.title: The request and the flow
docs.text:
A provider reads two mappings from the request: query, the URL parameters (the IdP's callback arrives there), and form, the decoded POST fields (a password login arrives there). A binding passes its native request when it has both, or a small wrapper:

from dataclasses import dataclass, field
from collections.abc import Mapping


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Request:
    query: Mapping[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)
    form: Mapping[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

LoginFlow holds the providers by ID, a TransactionStore and the allowed return_to prefixes:

from datetime import timedelta

from rn_forge.auth import InMemoryTransactionStore, LoginFlow

flow = LoginFlow(
    {"acme": acme_provider},
    InMemoryTransactionStore(),
    return_to_prefixes=["/app"],
    ttl=timedelta(seconds=600),  # the default
)

A binding mounts two routes over it:

# GET /auth/login/acme?return_to=/app/orders
start = flow.begin("acme", request, return_to="/app/orders")
# Set a cookie holding start.transaction.id; redirect to start.redirect_url.

# GET /auth/callback/acme
login = flow.complete("acme", request, transaction_id=cookie_value)
# login.identity is the verified identity; login.return_to is where to send
# the user. Clear the cookie, resolve the account, start the session.

begin checks return_to with validate_return_to, asks the provider for the redirect, and saves the transaction for the TTL. complete consumes the transaction first, so a callback works once whatever its outcome, then rejects a missing, expired, already used or foreign transaction (one that another provider began) before the provider sees the response. The transaction cookie is __Host-login-tx with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Lax, Path=/ and Max-Age=600: Lax sends it on the IdP's top-level redirect back, and the __Host- prefix stops a sibling subdomain from planting one. Reject a callback that carries more than one. Because the transaction binds the callback to the browser that started it, a callback replayed in another browser fails.

Every failure is one exception, LoginFailed, with a code from CallbackError: login_failed, or access_denied when the IdP returned error=access_denied. Send the code to the error route and keep reason in the logs; it names the failed check and must not reach the user. An invalid return_to and an unknown provider are login_failed too. Any other exception a provider raises is logged and also becomes login_failed.

docs.title: OIDC
docs.text:
from rn_forge.auth.oidc import OidcProvider

acme_provider = OidcProvider(
    id="acme",
    issuer="https://login.acme.example",
    client_id="orders-web",
    client_secret="...",
    redirect_uri="https://app.example/auth/callback/acme",
)

The provider reads the discovery document on first use and checks that it names the configured issuer. It sends state, a nonce and a PKCE S256 challenge, and records all three, with the verifier, on the transaction. On the callback it requires the same state, then checks the iss parameter (RFC 9207): a different iss fails, and a missing one fails when discovery advertises authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported. It then exchanges the code and verifies the ID token with IdTokenVerifier, including the nonce and at_hash. The secrets stay out of the logs.

Argument Effect scopes Defaults to openid email profile; openid is required max_age Sent on the authorization request; an ID token whose auth_time is older fails userinfo "auto" (default) calls UserInfo when the ID token has no email; "always" and "never" do as named. The UserInfo sub must equal the ID token's, and the ID token wins any other conflict claim_mapper Replaces default_claim_mapper token_hook Receives the identity and the upstream tokens rp_initiated_logout Lets logout_redirect return the IdP's logout URL token_endpoint_auth_method client_secret_basic by default; a public client (client_secret=None) sends none algorithms, leeway, timeout, fetch The accepted ID-token algorithms (RS256), clock skew, the back-channel timeout, and the discovery transport

docs.title: Claim mapping
docs.text:
default_claim_mapper fills sub, email, email_verified, name, picture, groups, auth_time and amr, takes sid as session_ref, and puts the remaining claims, except the token-protocol ones, in attributes. To change that, pass a function of the provider ID and the verified claims. It may raise LoginFailed to refuse the login:

from rn_forge.auth import ExternalIdentity, LoginFailed
from rn_forge.auth.oidc import default_claim_mapper


def acme_mapper(provider: str, claims):
    identity = default_claim_mapper(provider, claims)
    if not identity.email_verified:
        raise LoginFailed("login_failed", "email is not verified")
    return identity

docs.title: Upstream tokens
docs.text:
pykit stores no upstream token. The access and refresh tokens are dropped after the exchange unless the application passes a token_hook, which is called once the login has succeeded:

def keep_tokens(identity, tokens):  # tokens is an UpstreamTokens
    vault.save(identity.issuer, identity.subject, tokens.refresh_token)

The tokens have no repr, so a logged UpstreamTokens does not leak them.

docs.title: Logout
docs.text: With rp_initiated_logout=True, logout_redirect(session, post_logout_redirect=...) returns the discovered end_session_endpoint with id_token_hint, post_logout_redirect_uri and client_id. It returns None, and the binding logs out locally only, when the flag is off, the provider advertises no endpoint, or the session kept no ID token. A session keeps its ID token (SessionInfo.id_token) only when the application enables RP-initiated logout: with the flag on, the provider sets ExternalIdentity.id_token and the binding copies it into the session; with it off the field stays None. Signing out of the app does not normally need to sign the user out of their whole IdP session, so the flag is off by default.

docs.title: OAuth 2.0 providers
docs.text:
A server that issues no ID token, such as GitHub, uses OidcProvider.oauth2 with explicit endpoints and a fixed issuer string. The flow keeps state and PKCE, sends no nonce, and calls the user endpoint with the access token:

from rn_forge.auth import ExternalIdentity
from rn_forge.auth.oidc import OAuth2Endpoints, OidcProvider


def github_mapper(provider, claims):
    return ExternalIdentity(
        provider=provider,
        issuer=claims["iss"],
        subject=claims["sub"],
        email=claims.get("email"),
        name=claims.get("name"),
        picture=claims.get("avatar_url"),
    )


github = OidcProvider.oauth2(
    id="github",
    issuer="https://github.com",
    endpoints=OAuth2Endpoints(
        authorization="https://github.com/login/oauth/authorize",
        token="https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token",
        user="https://api.github.com/user",
    ),
    client_id="...",
    client_secret="...",
    redirect_uri="https://app.example/auth/callback/github",
    scopes=["read:user", "user:email"],
    subject_field="id",
    claim_mapper=github_mapper,
)

The user endpoint's JSON object becomes the claim set, with iss set to issuer and sub set to the subject_field member as a string, so GitHub's numeric id works. A user without that member fails the login. The default mapper reads the standard names; a provider with other names (avatar_url here) needs a mapper. The iss response check applies only when you pass response_issuer, because most OAuth 2.0 servers send none. Such a provider has no ID token to keep, so logout_redirect returns None, and token_hook receives UpstreamTokens with id_token=None. A failed user call, an HTTP error or a non-object body is login_failed.

docs.title: Back-channel logout
docs.text:
When the user signs out at the IdP, it posts a logout token to the application. BackchannelLogout validates it under the logout-token profile (see Token profiles) and says what to revoke:

from rn_forge.auth import InMemoryReplayStore
from rn_forge.auth.oidc import BackchannelLogout, LogoutTokenVerifier

replay = InMemoryReplayStore()
logout = BackchannelLogout(
    LogoutTokenVerifier.from_issuer(
        "https://login.acme.example", client_id="orders-web", replay_store=replay
    ),
    accounts,  # an AccountResolver; only lookup() is called
)

The binding mounts POST /auth/backchannel-logout/acme, reads the form field logout_token, and applies the result:

from rn_forge.auth.oidc import TokenVerificationError

try:
    revocation = logout.handle(form["logout_token"])
except TokenVerificationError:
    return response(400)
if revocation.sid is not None:
    replay.revoke_sid(revocation.issuer, revocation.sid, ttl=SESSION_ABSOLUTE_TIMEOUT)
elif revocation.account_id is not None:
    account_state.bump_session_version(revocation.account_id)
return response(200)

The handler changes no state of its own except the token's jti record, because the revoked-sid lifetime (the sessions' absolute timeout) and the session-version store belong to the binding. A token with a sid revokes that session only. A token with only sub names the account linked to (issuer, sub) through AccountResolver.lookup, whose session version the binding bumps; an unlinked sub gives account_id=None and nothing to do. Answer a failed token with 400 and log the exception message, which says which check failed.

docs.title: Password login
docs.text:
PasswordIdentityProvider needs no extra. The application supplies a verifier that returns the account's stable subject, or None for an unknown account or a wrong password:

from rn_forge.auth.local import PasswordIdentityProvider


def verify(username: str, password: str) -> str | None:
    account = accounts_by_name.get(username)
    return account.id if account and hasher.check(password, account.hash) else None


password = PasswordIdentityProvider(verify)  # id="password"

begin returns a transaction and no redirect, since the login is a form. The login page posts username and password, and the binding calls complete with those form fields. The identity has issuer local and amr of {"pwd"}. An unknown account and a wrong password fail with the same LoginFailed. Rate limiting per account and per client belongs to the binding, and the provider never logs or keeps the password. SSO or passkeys are preferred in production.

docs.title: Development login
docs.text:
DevelopmentIdentityProvider lists fixture accounts so that a developer, or an end-to-end test, signs in without a password. Construction raises DevelopmentModeRequired unless the caller passes debug=True; wire it to the framework's debug flag, never to a constant:

from rn_forge.auth.local import DevelopmentAccount, DevelopmentIdentityProvider

dev = DevelopmentIdentityProvider(
    [
        DevelopmentAccount("alice", email="alice@example.com", name="Alice"),
        DevelopmentAccount("bob", groups=frozenset({"staff"})),
    ],
    debug=settings.DEBUG,
)
html = dev.render_accounts(login_url="/auth/login/development")

render_accounts returns this markup, with every value HTML-escaped; an end-to-end test can rely on the attributes:

<ul data-rn-forge-dev-accounts>
<li><a href="/auth/login/development?account=alice" data-account="alice">Alice</a></li>
</ul>

The link text is the account's name, or its subject when it has none. The provider accepts the account as the account form field or query parameter, so a test can sign in directly. The identity has issuer development and amr of {"dev"}. An unknown account fails with LoginFailed.

docs.title: Connecting a SAML IdP through a broker
docs.text:
pykit speaks no SAML. A SAML IdP federates through a broker (Keycloak, Entra ID, Auth0, Okta and others), which runs the SAML exchange and then logs the user in to the application over OIDC. The application configures the broker as one ordinary OidcProvider; the SAML connection is the broker's configuration, not the application's. Most workforce IdPs also speak OIDC, and a direct connection to them needs no broker.

With Keycloak:

  1. Create a realm for the application and an OpenID Connect client in it (a confidential client with the standard flow, your callback URL as a valid redirect URI, and a secret).
  2. Under identity providers, add a SAML v2.0 provider with an alias such as saml-idp. Give it the SAML IdP's entity ID and single sign-on URL, and require signed assertions. Import the IdP's metadata when it publishes it.
  3. Add attribute mappers from the SAML attributes to user attributes (email, firstName, lastName), so that they reach the ID token as claims.
  4. Configure OidcProvider with the realm's issuer, https://<host>/realms/<realm>, and the client's ID and secret. To send users straight to the SAML IdP, add Keycloak's kc_idp_hint=saml-idp parameter to the redirect URL.
broker = OidcProvider(
    id="keycloak",
    issuer="https://sso.example/realms/acme",
    client_id="orders-web",
    client_secret="...",
    redirect_uri="https://app.example/auth/callback/keycloak",
)

The identity's issuer is the broker, and its subject is the broker's user ID, so an account links to (broker issuer, broker subject) whichever IdP the user signed in through. The SAML assertion is the broker's to validate; the application sees only the broker's signed ID token. tests/broker/ holds a working configuration: realms/idp-realm.json is a SAML IdP, and realms/broker-realm.json is a broker realm with the client, the SAML identity provider and the attribute mappers above. Testing describes how to run them.

docs.title: Stores
docs.text:
Four protocols hold server-side state. Each has an in-memory implementation in the core and a Redis implementation in rn_forge.auth.redis.

Protocol Holds Redis operation it relies on TransactionStore Login transactions between the redirect and the callback. consume returns the transaction to exactly one caller. SET ... EX to save, GETDEL to consume SessionStore Login sessions under random IDs. create, get, touch, delete and rotate. SET ... EX, GET, EXPIRE, GETDEL ReplayStore Single-use values, such as logout-token jti, and revoked (issuer, sid) pairs. SET key 1 NX EX for record_once, SET ... EX and EXISTS for revoked sid values AuthorizationVersions The counters behind AuthorizationContextCache. INCR per account and for the global counter, MGET to read

A session ends at its idle expiry or at SessionInfo.expires_at, whichever comes first. get does not extend the idle expiry, so a poll cannot keep an idle session alive; touch extends it, never past expires_at. rotate returns a new ID and leaves the old one unreadable. The stores do not check session versions or revoked sid values; the framework binding does that after get.

from redis import Redis
from rn_forge.auth.redis import RedisSessionStore, RedisTransactionStore

client = Redis.from_url("redis://localhost:6379/0")
sessions = RedisSessionStore(client)
transactions = RedisTransactionStore(client, prefix="myapp-auth:")

session_id = sessions.create(session_info, idle_ttl=timedelta(minutes=30))

docs.title: Supported storage
docs.text:
Transactions, replay records and revoked sid values must be shared by every worker, so a store used by more than one process must be backed by shared storage whose operations above are atomic. The in-memory stores (InMemoryTransactionStore, InMemorySessionStore, InMemoryReplayStore and InMemoryAuthorizationVersions) are thread-safe but are not safe across processes; use them in tests and single-process development only. The Redis stores need Redis 6.2 or later (for GETDEL).

Every Redis store takes a client and a key prefix ("rn-forge-auth:" by default). Expiries are whole seconds, rounded up, and at least one. A session is stored as JSON, and a missing, expired or rotated-away key reads as absent.

docs.title: Authorization versions
docs.text: AuthorizationVersions holds the counters behind AuthorizationContextCache (see Contracts): a version per account and a global version, read together by current(account_id) and raised by bump(account_id) and bump_all(). InMemoryAuthorizationVersions is local to the process, so with several workers a bump reaches only the worker that made it and the others rely on the cache TTL. RedisAuthorizationVersions shares the counters through INCR and MGET.

docs.title: Testing with the fake IdP
docs.text:
rn_forge.auth.testing.FakeOidcProvider is an OIDC provider that runs inside the test process on 127.0.0.1 and an ephemeral port, so a test needs no network. It needs the oidc extra and, like rn_forge.auth.oidc, is imported directly. It serves discovery, a key set, an authorization endpoint that approves a configured user without a login page, a token endpoint that checks PKCE and client authentication, and UserInfo.

from rn_forge.auth.oidc import IdTokenVerifier
from rn_forge.auth.testing import FakeOidcProvider

with FakeOidcProvider(redirect_uris=["http://127.0.0.1/callback"]) as idp:
    verifier = IdTokenVerifier.from_issuer(idp.issuer, client_id=idp.client_id)
    # Drive idp.authorization_endpoint and idp.token_endpoint, then:
    claims = verifier.verify(id_token, nonce=nonce, access_token=access_token)

In pytest, wrap it in a fixture:

@pytest.fixture
def idp():
    with FakeOidcProvider() as provider:
        yield provider

Authorization codes are single use, and a PKCE verifier that does not match the challenge is refused. idp.requests lists every request as a RecordedRequest of method and path. idp.rotate_key(retire_old=...) adds a signing key, and idp.sign(...), idp.access_token(profile=...) and idp.logout_token(sid=...) mint tokens for the verifier profiles. Set idp.deny_authorization for an access_denied response, and idp.auth_age (seconds) to make the user's authentication older, which sets the ID token's auth_time.

To test an OAuth 2.0-only provider, set idp.oauth2_only = True. The authorization endpoint then needs no openid scope or nonce, the token response has no ID token, and the UserInfo endpoint (idp.userinfo_endpoint) serves as the user endpoint.

docs.title: Driving a login
docs.text: A test drives the browser leg with plain HTTP: it follows the authorization redirect, stops at the callback, and reads code, state and iss from the Location header. It then hands those parameters to LoginFlow.complete as the request's query.

docs.title: Failure switches
docs.text:
idp.faults is a Faults; every field is off by default and turns on one failure:

Field The provider then response_iss Sends an iss in the authorization response that names another issuer response_iss_missing Leaves iss out of the authorization response discovery_issuer Names another issuer in its discovery document userinfo_sub_mismatch Returns a UserInfo sub that differs from the ID token's userinfo_error Answers the UserInfo (user) endpoint with 500 wrong_nonce, wrong_aud, wrong_azp, wrong_at_hash Mints an ID token with that claim wrong expired Mints an ID token whose exp is past alg_none Mints an unsigned ID token unknown_kid Signs the ID token with a key the key set does not list

discover_oidc rejects discovery_issuer, and IdTokenVerifier rejects each ID-token switch. The iss response check, the UserInfo sub check and the UserInfo error belong to OidcProvider, not to a verifier.

docs.title: The broker profile
docs.text:
The fake covers the protocol; a real broker covers the configuration. The tests in tests/broker/ run OidcProvider against Keycloak: an OIDC login, a login federated from a SAML IdP inside Keycloak, and a client-credentials bearer call through OidcAuthenticator. They need Docker and are skipped unless RN_FORGE_AUTH_KEYCLOAK_URL is set:

docker compose -f packages/rn-forge-auth/tests/broker/compose.yml up -d --wait
RN_FORGE_AUTH_KEYCLOAK_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080 \
  uv run pytest packages/rn-forge-auth -m broker

The broker-profile workflow runs them weekly and on changes to this package. It is not a required check and does not gate merges. The realms under tests/broker/realms/ also serve as a working configuration for connecting a SAML IdP through a broker.

docs.title: Token profiles
docs.text: rn_forge.auth.oidc verifies JWTs for bearer authentication, the OIDC callback and back-channel logout. It needs the oidc extra and is imported directly. The core never imports it. The contracts it feeds are in Contracts; the in-process provider for testing it is in Testing.

docs.title: OIDC bearer tokens
docs.text:
OidcAuthenticator is an Authenticator for Bearer credentials. It verifies the token with a JwtVerifier, then maps the claims with claims_to_principal, which defaults to principal_from_claims. A scheme other than Bearer raises AuthenticationFailed.

Build it once at startup with discovery, which reads the issuer's /.well-known/openid-configuration:

from rn_forge.auth.oidc import OidcAuthenticator

authenticator = OidcAuthenticator.from_issuer(
    "https://login.example.com/",
    audience="orders-api",
)

Or pin the key-set URL and skip discovery, for an identity provider that publishes no discovery document:

authenticator = OidcAuthenticator.from_jwks_url(
    "https://login.example.com/keys",
    issuer="https://login.example.com/",
    audience="orders-api",
)

Discovery runs once, inside from_issuer; the authenticator then holds the key set cache, so reuse one instance rather than building one per request. The discovery document's issuer must equal the issuer it was fetched for, and a mismatch raises TokenVerificationError.

Verification requires exp, iss and aud as well as checking them. A token without exp is rejected rather than treated as non-expiring. The algorithms list, ("RS256",) by default, is an allow-list: a token whose header names another algorithm, including none, is rejected. The header must carry a kid. leeway tolerates clock skew, in seconds, on exp, nbf and iat.

docs.title: Token profiles
docs.text:
An identity provider issues several kinds of JWT, and each has its own verifier used at exactly one place. A token valid under one is never accepted by another.

Verifier Used at Accepts JwtVerifier Bearer authentication on API routes An access token. IdTokenVerifier The OIDC callback An ID token for your login client, checked against the nonce you sent. LogoutTokenVerifier The back-channel logout endpoint A logout token, accepted once.

JwtVerifier takes mode. With "rfc7519" (the default) it accepts a typ of JWT or none, requires iss, aud and exp, and validates sub, nbf and iat when present. With "rfc9068" it accepts only typ at+jwt or application/at+jwt and requires iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti. In both modes it rejects any token that carries nonce or events, which an ID token and a logout token do.

Pass your OIDC login client ID as login_client_id. An API audience equal to it is refused with ValueError unless mode="rfc9068", because otherwise an ID token issued to your login client would pass as an access token.

IdTokenVerifier.verify(token, nonce=..., access_token=...) checks signature, iss, aud, azp, exp, iat, nonce and, when an access token is given, at_hash. With max_age set, auth_time is required and must be no older than that many seconds.

LogoutTokenVerifier needs a ReplayStore, such as InMemoryReplayStore (one process only). It requires the back-channel logout event, a sid or sub, no nonce, an iat no older than max_age_seconds (120 by default), and a jti it has not accepted before. The jti is stored under "{iss}|{jti}" until the token expires, and only once every other check has passed.

All three build with from_issuer or from_jwks_url, and all refuse a key-set URL that is not HTTPS.

docs.title: The key-set cache
docs.text:
Signing keys come from PyJWT's PyJWKClient, configured by two options on from_issuer and from_jwks_url:

Option Default Meaning lifespan 300 seconds How long a fetched key set stays cached. cooldown_duration 30 seconds The fewest seconds between two key set fetches. A token with an unknown kid triggers a refetch only after this long.

The cooldown bounds how often a stream of tokens with unknown kid values can make the process call the identity provider.

docs.title: The HTTPS rule
docs.text: The adapter fetches key material only over HTTPS. Plain HTTP is accepted only for localhost, 127.0.0.1 and ::1, which is what a test server needs. fetch_json, which reads the discovery document, checks its URL, and the JWKS URL, whether it came from discovery or from from_jwks_url, is checked too; a violation raises TokenVerificationError. The fetch argument of from_issuer replaces fetch_json for the discovery document only, so a replacement transport owns the check on that one URL. The key set itself is always fetched by PyJWKClient.

docs.title: Failure reasons are for logs
docs.text: TokenVerificationError carries the specific reason a token, key set or discovery document failed: an expired token, an unknown kid, an audience mismatch. The reason is for logs. OidcAuthenticator re-raises it as AuthenticationFailed so the framework binding can log it, and the response body must never repeat it: a 401 body is AUTH_FAILED_DETAIL, so a caller cannot tell which check failed.

docs.title: Authentication and authorization
docs.text: The package has one core and two adapters. rn_forge.auth holds the contracts and needs no third-party package. rn_forge.auth.oidc runs OIDC and OAuth 2.0 logins and verifies OIDC bearer tokens (see Login providers), and rn_forge.auth.redis keeps sessions and single-use records in Redis; both import the core and the core never imports them. The oidc extra installs pyjwt[crypto] and authlib, the redis extra installs redis, and the rn_forge.auth facade re-exports neither adapter.

docs.title: How the pieces fit
docs.text:
A login and each later request pass through the same stages:

provider -> ExternalIdentity -> AccountResolver -> account ID
  -> session (SessionInfo) or bearer token
  -> AuthorizationContext -> Principal
  -> Requirement (route) -> ResourcePolicy (object and query)
  1. An IdentityProvider authenticates the user and returns an ExternalIdentity. The login is held in a TransactionStore while the browser is away.
  2. An AccountResolver maps the identity to an internal account ID, or rejects the login. A SessionStore then holds a SessionInfo under a random ID.
  3. On each request, a session or a verified bearer token identifies the account. An AuthorizationContextProvider, usually behind an AuthorizationContextCache, returns the account's current permissions, and the binding builds a Principal. For a bearer caller the token's scopes limit those permissions and never add to them.
  4. An Authorizer checks the route's Requirement against the Principal. A ResourcePolicy then checks the object, or narrows the query.
Guide Covers Contracts Identity, account resolution, authorization context and cache, Principal and Requirement, permissions and the scope limit, resource policy, return_to and the session body Token profiles JwtVerifier, IdTokenVerifier and LogoutTokenVerifier, modes, the login-client rule, key rotation and cooldown Stores The four store protocols, in-memory and Redis, and the atomic operation each relies on Testing FakeOidcProvider and its failure switches

docs.title: Installing
docs.text:
Declare the package from pykit's index, with the extras you use:

dependencies = ["rn-forge-auth[oidc,redis]>=0.1.0,<0.2"]

The base install, rn-forge-auth, is enough to write your own authenticator. Importing rn_forge.auth.oidc without the extra fails with ModuleNotFoundError for jwt. rn-forge-django[oidc] and rn-forge-fastapi[oidc] already name rn-forge-auth[oidc]. Importing rn_forge.auth.redis without the redis extra fails with ModuleNotFoundError for redis.

docs.title: With rn-forge-web and the framework packages
docs.text:
rn-forge-web owns the wire contract that surrounds these types:

  • Credentials, the raw scheme and token lifted off a request;
  • parse_authorization, which reads an Authorization header into Credentials;
  • challenge_header, which builds the WWW-Authenticate value;
  • AUTH_FAILED_DETAIL, the fixed 401 detail, "Authentication failed.";
  • the AuthenticationFailed and PermissionDenied exceptions.

This package adds the verified caller and the decisions made about it. A framework binding does the plumbing between them: it parses the header, calls the Authenticator, turns AuthenticationFailed into a 401 with a challenge and AUTH_FAILED_DETAIL, and turns PermissionDenied into a 403. rn-forge-django binds Principal to DRF with PrincipalBearerAuthentication, JWKSBearerAuthentication and requires; rn-forge-fastapi binds it with bearer_auth, basic_auth and requires. See those packages' guides for wiring.

OIDC: discovery, the login provider, one validation profile per kind of token (access, ID and logout) and the authenticator that maps verified access-token claims to a :class:~rn_forge.auth.Principal.

docs.text:
The access-token profile: verify a bearer JWT against a key set, an issuer and an audience.

mode="rfc9068" accepts only RFC 9068 access tokens: a typ header of at+jwt or application/at+jwt (case-insensitive), and iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti present. mode="rfc7519" accepts a typ of JWT (case-insensitive) or none, requires iss, aud and exp, and validates sub, nbf and iat when present.

An OIDC :class:~rn_forge.auth.IdentityProvider: authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), over Authlib's OAuth2Session.

docs.title: rn_forge.auth.testing
docs.text:
An in-process OpenID Connect provider for tests.

:class:FakeOidcProvider serves discovery, a key set with rotation, an authorization endpoint, a token endpoint, UserInfo and back-channel logout tokens on a loopback port. Nothing leaves the machine. Each field of :class:Faults switches one failure on.

Requires the oidc extra. Not imported by :mod:rn_forge.auth; import this module directly.

Example: >>> with FakeOidcProvider() as idp: ... idp.issuer.startswith("http://127.0.0.1:") True

docs.title: FakeOidcProvider(*, client_id='web-login', client_secret='fake-secret', redirect_uris=('http://127.0.0.1/callback',), user=None, tenant='tenant', id_token_ttl=300.0)
docs.text:
An OpenID Connect provider on 127.0.0.1 and an ephemeral port.

The issuer is http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<tenant>. The authorization endpoint approves user without a login page and redirects back with a single-use code; the token endpoint exchanges it, checking PKCE and the client's credentials. Use it as a context manager, or call :meth:start and :meth:close.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default client_id str

The registered client.

'web-login' client_secret str | None

The client's secret, accepted as client_secret_post or HTTP Basic. None registers a public client.

'fake-secret' redirect_uris Sequence[str]

The registered redirect URIs.

('http://127.0.0.1/callback',) user Mapping[str, Any] | None

The claims of the user the authorization endpoint approves; it must contain sub.

None tenant str

The issuer's path segment.

'tenant' id_token_ttl float

Seconds an ID token or an access token stays valid.

300.0

Attributes:

Name Type Description faults

The failure switches; assign :class:Faults or set fields.

deny_authorization

When true the authorization endpoint answers access_denied instead of approving.

oauth2_only

When true the provider behaves as a plain OAuth 2.0 server: the authorization endpoint accepts a request without the openid scope or a nonce, and the token response carries no ID token. The UserInfo endpoint then serves as the user endpoint.

advertise_end_session

Whether discovery lists end_session_endpoint.

auth_age

Seconds before each authorization request that the approved user is recorded as having authenticated; it sets the ID token's auth_time.

requests list[RecordedRequest]

Every request received, in order.

issuer

The issuer URL.

jwks_url

Where the key set is served.

docs.text:
A signed JWT access token for bearer tests.

rfc9068 carries typ: at+jwt and iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti. rfc7519 carries no typ and only iss, exp, aud, sub and iat. Extra claims override those; a claim set to None is omitted.

The ID token's at_hash is not the access token's hash.

The ID token's exp is in the past.

The ID token is unsigned (alg: none).

The ID token is signed with a key the key set does not list, under a kid it does not list.
